title: Support hotpatching systems
body:
## What problem does this solve or what need does it fill?

A common complaint from Bevy users is the relatively high iteration time. Hotpatching is a nice solution for this, as it allows code changes to affect the running binary.

## What solution would you like?

While many things can be hotpatched, I think implementing it for systems is a nice start. This way, users could already start live-editing their UIs by changing a system that re-inserts a UI node hierarchy in `Update`, for example.

## What alternative(s) have you considered?

- Don't implement it
- Start with hotpatching another area of Bevy
- Leave it to third-party crates like dextrous-developer

## Additional context

Recently, [Dioxus has released](https://github.com/DioxusLabs/dioxus/releases/tag/v0.7.0-alpha.0) an alpha of  [subsecond](https://github.com/DioxusLabs/dioxus/tree/main/packages/subsecond), which implements exactly this. One of their explicit goals is to make this technology available for other frameworks such as Bevy.
If we go this route, there is already a [Bevy integration demo](https://github.com/participant3/subsecond-bevy-demo). Per @participant3, this is not meant as a long-term end-user API, but to give Bevy maintainers and early adopters today an example of how to wire stuff up. We need to spend some time working on the integration between the two, in order to ensure it is safe.

comments.author: participant6
comments.body:
> wasm-bindgen, wasm-pack, and trunk are not cargo subcommands. cargo cannot `run`, `test`, or `bench` wasm, ios, android projects nor does it properly assemble app bundles. wasm-bindgen is the most used cli in the rust ecosystem and it is not a subcommand.

@participant3 I'd argue it still makes sense as a subcommand, even though others aren't. Cargo subcommands are basically the same as git subcommands - they just attach a prefix, and your binary works the same as standalone. The only difference (from a rudimentary check of making one) is that they automatically set some environment variables in addition, specifically:

- `CARGO_HOME` - `$HOME/.cargo` usually
- `RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN` - current target triple
- `SSL_CERT_DIR` - in my case, `/etc/ssl/certs`
- `SSL_CERT_FILE` - in my case, `/etc/ssl/cert.pem`
- `RUST_RECURSION_COUNT` - just a general recursion counter
- `RUSTUP_HOME` - `$HOME/.rustup` usually
- `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` - it injects the current rust toolchain lib dir
- `CARGO` - Full path to the cargo binary for the current active toolchain

as well as adding the actual cargo subcommand name as the first argument.

In the case of the standard dx CLI, it makes sense to be standalone - dioxus is not just a rust tool, and can be initialized via npm too. So requiring it be a cargo subcommand may be a little constraining.
On the flipside, the cargo subcommands do work without cargo, as they are just named as `cargo-binname` so you can run it as that. For a rust ecosystem tool, I think it makes more sense for it to be a cargo subcommand, if we are trying to make it widely reusable as the dioxus project seems to hope for. The dx cli can just inject what it needs into the argument list when running as a subcommand, assuming that's how you guys would integrate it if it were to be split out.

Many cargo-installed binaries I use don't work as a cargo subcommand, but generally the differentiator between ones that do and ones that don't are if they are specifically about rust code and operating on your actual codebase (with the exception of cargo-install-update, which is a cargo subcommand but doesn't operate on a codebase level - still makes sense to me).
I'd argue that a subsecond CLI tool makes a lot of sense as a cargo subcommand, given the general pattern I've seen.

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
Re: cargo subcommand vs own command

The frustrations with cargo's limitations and its glacial development cycle has led this very project to design the Bevy CLI alpha as a cargo replacement / wrapper and not a subcommand.

I think it's worth not immediately dismissing the validity of a cargo v2. As Jon points out, quite a few projects have come to the conclusion that cargo is often simply not enough. The discussion of whether we want to collectively encourage the ecosystem to migrate to a cargo replacement or not is certainly out of scope for this wee issue. For prolonged discussion of this, I suggest moving to a dedicated issue on the Dioxus repo instead.

For Bevy's use-case, the relevant PR is not even merged yet, the feature is experimental, and the Dioxus version it depends on is in alpha. Really, we should be fine with some hoops right now IMO.

comments.body:
> There are bugs and dragons abound and big work ahead like proper workspace support. Lots of sweat and long nights went into this, hand-rolled assembly, and head banging to figure out esoteric hacks to get it working. From what I understand, the `bevy_cli` is largely a standalone tool (rather than a `cargo` subcommand) because it needs to support custom lints (an important upstream goal), and to ensure that we can easily bundle all sorts of weird functionality that only matters for the game dev use case.

I'm a bit concerned about the notion of a "cargo plus plus". I really appreciate how unified the Rust ecosystem is here, and the upstream `cargo` team has been really supportive of efforts to meet the needs of its users, including GUI folks.

That said, the existing `dx` experience has quite a bit of additional polish and refinement over the `bevy_cli`, even ignoring hotpatching. I'm not sure if a shared frontend makes sense across different frameworks (how do you only grab the components you want?), but that's just a technical question of exactly where we should be drawing a split. I'm very much interested in sharing as much infrastructure there as possible: I think we have a lot of shared goals.

> It's understandable if some random fly-by contributor did this, but the head of another large rust project doing it without even reaching out is disappointing.

I understand your frustration here. From the Bevy side, none of the Bevy maintainers are currently involved in the immediate forking effort, but we have requested a better separation between the subsecond work and the main dioxus framework, in order to better enable collaboration on hotpatching. We wouldn't expect (or want!) merge rights or say in the direction of Dioxus itself, and it really would make issue tracking and contributions easier.

comments.author: participant7
comments.body:
> > The frustrations with cargo's limitations and its glacial development cycle has led this very project to design the Bevy CLI alpha as a cargo replacement / wrapper and not a subcommand.
> > 
> > I think it's worth not immediately dismissing the validity of a cargo v2. As Jon points out, quite a few projects have come to the conclusion that cargo is often simply not enough. The discussion of whether we want to collectively encourage the ecosystem to migrate to a cargo replacement or not is certainly out of scope for this wee issue. For prolonged discussion of this, I suggest moving to a dedicated issue on the Dioxus repo instead.
>
> reporter I am kinda curious - what were the limitations found? Do you have a link to a discussion on the discord or here on github about this? I'm unaware of such limitations as I don't tend to work on CLI tools much, so I'm very interested where the limitations have been found.

I have a slightly different interpretation than Jan as to why the Bevy CLI was created. In my opinion, Bevy has specific needs that wouldn't fit in a general-purpose, stable tool like Cargo. One of the largest examples of this is [Bevy CLI's web feature](https://thebevyflock.github.io/bevy_cli/cli/web.html), which lets you build, bundle, and test Bevy apps for the web. This kind of feature doesn't fit in base Cargo as the Bevy CLI performs special Bevy-specific logic, such as how it handles assets and the default `index.html`.

From my perspective, it's less that Cargo is _lacking_ features and more that certain features are too specific to be included in a standard Rust distribution. In my opinion, it's better to be able to build off of Cargo with 3rd-party tools than have Cargo implement features that only work for a small subset of the ecosystem.

I personally don't mind Cargo's slow pace. The Cargo maintainers are careful, and are targeting a _much_ larger audience than Bevy's game devs and Dioxus's web devs. They encourage building tools on top of Cargo, that's why they have shortcuts for `cargo-foo` -> `cargo foo` and spin out so much of their logic into reusable libraries.

comments.author: participant8
comments.body:
The Dioxus folks have put a lot of effort into building a useful tool. I think it is _extremely_ reasonable for them to want people using that tool to know it came from them (aka preserving the Dioxus / `dx` branding). We attach the Bevy brand to _many_ of our "general purpose" libraries (Bevy ECS, Bevy Reflect, etc) for the same reason.

If someone were to publish a "debranded" Bevy Reflect without discussing it with us, I would consider that bad form. Legal according to the license, but bad form nonetheless. Imagine the consequences of that library taking over. We would keep doing work to improve things over in Bevy land, but some of the "social capital" and positive public opinion would attrit to the debranded fork instead (the more adoption the fork gets, the more this would be true). Perhaps we get fewer donations because the people who would have supported an open source general purpose Rust reflection library now donate elsewhere. Over time, perhaps we lose our ability to invest developer time in it completely.

I think the Bevy Reflect case is _extremely_ relevant here. There is incredible demand for a general purpose Rust reflection library. But many people see Bevy as a competitor in their space that they couldn't possibly depend on / associate with. Many also see us as a "big" framework that they don't want to pull in. Bevy Reflect is standalone / does not pull in the rest of Bevy, but the perception alone is enough to keep some people away.

In practice this has resulted in pretty much nobody taking a dependency on Bevy Reflect, despite us pioneering in the space _for years_. To my knowledge I was the first person to build such a library in Rust. But time and time again when a big project could have depended on Bevy Reflect, they chose to build a competitor that largely just copied our techniques (Embark, Fyrox, etc). I think the choice to include the Bevy branding here played a big part (but I also concede that taking dependencies is always a complex decision). If we had developed it under a different name and/or under a different "more neutral" org, I strongly suspect we would have been able to appeal to more projects, and perhaps today we would be the "go to" general purpose Rust reflection library. Instead, the new kid on the block Facet will likely occupy that position. I do not think it is a coincidence that Facet is decoupled from a specific "large framework" brand and that it lives on "neutral" ground (its own org).

As an aside, note that I think Facet _is_ probably the better choice for the "general purpose reflection space" at this point, and they are _not_ just a copy of Bevy Reflect. I also think Facet is the better general purpose reflection library because _that is what it set out to do_. Bevy Reflect _was_ built with our needs in mind, and that _has_ resulted in different design decisions (some of which may not have been accepted on more "neutral" ground). I doubt we will switch to Facet (at least not for a long while), as we have a ton of unique use cases where Bevy Reflect serves us better.

I think the parallels between Bevy Reflect and Dioxus' Subsecond (which most end-users will generally know as `dx serve --hot-patch`) are clear. I will not make any recommendations or prescriptions here.

With my "Bevy project lead" hat on, these are the things I want to balance:
* I want cool projects to succeed and the people that build them to get paid
* When taking a dependency, I want the smallest "chain of trust" possible. I want to consume a dependency directly through its developer, not a third party intermediary.
* If a dependency is particularly valuable, I want our users to know that we depend on it (we give visibility to our "big" dependencies like wgpu and winit in a number of places).
* I want Bevy to feel like a cohesive "one stop shop" experience (ex: download the rust tool chain, install bevy, you're good to go). People shouldn't need to install 10 different command line tools to get the best experience.
* I don't want people to conflate Bevy apps with Dioxus apps (note that we are also a general purpose UI framework), both for branding / "project health" reasons and "user cognitive load" reasons.

In the context of hot patching, I think that positions us in the following way:

* For as long as Dioxus is the primary developer of the "interesting" technical bits of the hot reloading codebase, I want to consume those things directly from them, and in a way that leaves us on good, collaborative terms (provided Dioxus' implementation can meet our needs, and the needs of our users, and we feel like there is a collaborative relationship that reacts to the Bevy project's needs). 
* If that means not building "neutral" (or Bevy-specific) subsecond or `dx` wrappers, so be it. But know that this is a pretty major concession when it comes to our "ideal user experience" _and_ the Bevy vs Dioxus app conflation issue. 
* If a competitor were to emerge that provides a similar experience, brings similar "developer expertise" to the table (aka they aren't just copying/debranding Dioxus code, and I have confidence in their skillset), and that project was ok with us building our own branded developer experience on top (or a more neutral experience), I would heavily consider moving to such a project, as that would be the better constraint solve for us (and our users).

I suspect that other developers will feel the same, and many projects won't have the same scruples we do when it comes to "healthy, mutually beneficial collaboration". Dioxus has pioneered a truly wonderful Rust developer experience and pretty much every major Rust project is going to want it for their users. I suspect that a "best fit" solution for all Rust projects _will_ emerge eventually, whatever that means.

(@participant3, @participant2, @participant1)

comments.author: participant2
comments.body:
@participant8 I see things differently. If someone took something like `iced_wgpu` and turned it into a generic 2D renderer, I'd honestly be thrilled and flattered.

I'm strongly against the idea of "branding" in open source, specially when it gets in the way of broader adoption and general-purpose use. It creates conflicting expectations, discourages collaboration across projects, and can ultimately hurt users of the wider ecosystem. Bevy Reflect being a perfect example of this, as you pointed out.

Improving and sharing existing code with others is at the heart of open source. Framing that as "bad form" goes against its very essence. Alternatives usually add value—even if they create fragmentation, that's often outweighed by the diversity and innovation they bring. Open source isn't a zero-sum game.

Of course, credit matters and I make it a point to be very open about my dependencies in all of my projects; specially if I am modifying code directly. You bet I will mention Dioxus in `iced` if we start using `subsecond`.

In any case, it seems we fundamentally disagree on what open source is about, so I am afraid we may not find much common ground here.

I will just restate that I don't have any ill intent. I'm not trying to take credit nor seek attention—my projects have little to no marketing, I barely have any social presence, and I honestly want none of it. I'm just focused on building useful tools.

For this reason, I will remove any unnecessary branding when it may benefit me, my users, or the ecosystem. Whether that's seen as bad form is up to others—but my doors to collaboration will always remain open.

comments.author: participant8
comments.body:
> In any case, it seems we fundamentally disagree on what open source is about, so I am afraid we may not find much common ground here.

I'm sure that isn't true :)

I share your ideals in a number of categories:
* Open source not being a zero sum game (although I think it is somewhere on the spectrum between zero sum and the reverse)
* Open source being about collaboration
* Forking often being a good thing in the ecosystem
* Open source being about "collective ownership". We are contributing to the commons, to the benefit of all _and_ (largely) without restriction. Everyone is free to do what they want. I will just assert that _sometimes_ "doing what you want" has negative implications for the social and economic state of the ecosystem. 

I think where we disagree is probably in areas like "open source social dynamics" and "open source project funding". Forking a project is not fully non-zero sum. There is only so much oxygen in the room at a given point (there are only so many people in a given space, and they only have so many hours in the day). And if you publicly fork a project, that is (to a degree) using the work of the developers of that project to compete with itself.

If you are fully enlightened you might be able to feel nothing but goodwill for a fork of a project like `iced` that pulls all of your changes, tweaks a few things, and takes the majority of your users (and thus some of the incentives that motivate many of us, such as human connection, words of encouragement, "social credit", and putting food on our table). But many of us humans would feel a bit hurt by that. And the humans developing that project (depending on the context) might consider that "anti-collaborative", as you are choosing to "take up space" with your fork (and benefit from their work), rather than collaborate under a given banner. These banners are "brands", or "collective identities", for better or for worse.

A big part of open source is about _who_ is holding a banner up, _what_ their values are, and _how_ they collaborate. Not all banners are worth collaborating under. For me, _that_ is where forking comes in, and that is where the open source model really shows its resilience. But I consider "public long running forks" to be a method of last resort. It is a sign that collaboration under a given banner has broken down. It is a signal that others should join you under your banner _instead_. That you are not willing to work under the terms of someone else's banner. That is your right. But just like other "rights", such as freedom of speech, sometimes exercising your right is a net negative on your community.

Open source software is not "just" about "software freedom". It is the people that build it, the values they share, and the systems that fuel them. It is an ecosystem. It is a community. Forks _very clearly_ have an effect on that ecosystem, and those effects are complicated (sometimes positive, sometimes negative, but pretty much always both). The ecosystem consists of "productive actions" (adding to the commons) and "consumptive actions" (taking from the commons / making demands of it). Most actions we take can be framed somewhere on that spectrum (what are we "giving" and what are we "taking"). Yes, cloning code is "free", and when considered in a vacuum ... not zero sum. But public forking is more than just a "clone action" (as mentioned above).

I am of the mind that "producers" should be rewarded for their efforts via the various levers mentioned above. For me, _part_ of that is choosing to collaborate under banners even when they aren't 100% perfect for me. Especially in cases where I am taking on more of a "consumer" role.

comments.author: participant2
comments.body:
> Forking a project is not fully zero sum. There is only so much oxygen in the room at a given point (there are only so many people in a given space, and they only have so many hours in the day). And if you publicly fork a project, that is (to a degree) using the work of the developers of that project to compete with itself.

I don't think it's that simple. Open source isn't a single room with limited space. Forking creates a new room and can bring new people, it can reduce conflict, and make the community in each room have a stronger focus, work better, and produce more value.

> If you are fully enlightened you might be able to feel nothing but goodwill for a fork of a project like iced that pulls all of your changes, tweaks a few things, and takes the majority of your users

Hard forks do not generally happen over a "few tweaks".

The only way this could happen is if `iced` deliberately kept these tweaks away from the majority of its users. A fork is only possible if you let yourself get forked.

I would probably adopt these tweaks in this case, unless they went completely against the philosophy of the library. But then, it would not be just "a few tweaks" anymore; and the communities would be better off branching out rather than constantly arguing over foundational concepts.

> But many of us humans would feel a bit hurt by that. And the humans developing that project (depending on the context) might consider that "anti-collaborative", as you are choosing to "take up space" with your fork (and benefit from their work), rather than collaborate under a given banner. These banners are "brands", or "collective identities", for better or for worse.

I understand that, but I don't think it's reasonable. These "brands" and "collective identities" encourage tribalism mixed together with a bunch of entitlement and expectations. As Rich Hickey puts it:

> Open source is a licensing and delivery mechanism, period. It means you get the source for software and the right to use and modify it. All social impositions associated with it, including the idea of 'community-driven-development' are part of a recently-invented mythology with little basis in how things actually work, a mythology that embodies, cult-like, both a lack of support for diversity in the ways things can work and a pervasive sense of communal entitlement.
>
> — Rich Hickey, [Open Source is Not About You](https://gist.github.com/richhickey/1563cddea1002958f96e7ba9519972d9)

In any case, it seems your argument comes down to "us humans" being inherently flawed or unreasonable. While that may be the case, it doesn't really justify bad behavior. In fact, it seems to be a self-defeating argument. Unless you were mocking me, shouldn't we strive to be like the truly enlightened ones?

> I am of the mind that "producers" should be rewarded for their efforts via the various levers mentioned above. For me, part of that is choosing to collaborate under banners even when they aren't 100% perfect for me. Especially in cases where I am taking on more of a "consumer" role.

I think this is the core issue. I don't think "producers" of open source should be entitled to anything; the same way "consumers" aren't either. This is the real beauty of open source—a gift with no expectations.

comments.author: participant8
comments.body:
> I understand that, but I don't think it's reasonable. These "brands" and "collective identities" encourage tribalism mixed together with a bunch of entitlement and expectations. As Rich Hickey puts it:

Collaboration is inherently political (and therefore tribal). We will come up with words (and yes banners) to (lossily) describe our values, and choose which banners to work under that describe our values. Banners (and the organizations behind them) will rise and fall based on public sentiment / approval. I believe a healthy ecosystem is one where we don't cling too tightly to any given banner, but are also willing to make concessions to collaborate under banners that aren't perfect for us (because otherwise we will all just work alone).

> are part of a recently-invented mythology with little basis in how things actually work

Make a list of your most used open source projects. Each project in that list is almost certainly built by a "tribe" that has rules, codes of conduct, social dynamics, etc. That tribe will have a name and a logo. There will be zealots (which should be discouraged), but most of the developers are likely just pragmatic, good natured people trying to better their lives, and the lives of those around them.

Imagine a world where those projects had no name, no formal organization, no codes of conduct, no common banner. Is that a better world? Notably, its not the world that has been constructed for `iced`, which has all of those things. I would be curious (and excited) to see what that looks like!

> Unless you were mocking me, shouldn't we strive to be like the truly enlightened ones?

I am definitely not mocking you. "Enlightenment" is a tricky beast, and hard to talk about in concrete terms. From my perspective it means (among many other things) cultivating a loving and generous heart, eliminating ego, and letting go of your attachments (or at least, no longer clinging to them). I think these are all noble endeavors and we _should_ strive for them.

But things start to fall apart when you try to take enlightenment into the real world. What concessions will you make to put food on your table, your family's table, or your community's? What things will you cling to? Do you "work" in open source? If you do, might that change how you relate to it? If you don't, are you living an enlightened life in your current job?

Do you think people _should_ "work" in open source at all?

> I think this is the core issue. I don't think "producers" of open source should be entitled to anything; the same way "consumers" aren't either. This is the real beauty of open source—a gift with no expectations.

To reframe this, what if this wasn't about what the "producer" is _entitled_ to, but rather how you think you should treat them? Should someone giving away free gifts be treated with respect and collaborated with, or competed with? Would you try to consider their human feelings (and not operate under the assumption that they are fully enlightened?). Would an enlightened person comport themselves as if everyone else is enlightened?

This has become very philosophical, which is awesome. But this is also not really the place to hash these things out (and its the kind of thing many people will have opinions on). Feel free to leave one more response to what I've said, but I'll refrain from responding further on these more abstract issues, and I will ask that everyone else does the same, in the interest of this thread not devolving.  (edit: but feel free to reach out to me if you want to talk about this more one on one)

comments.author: participant2
comments.body:
I think we are talking past each other a bit.

We interact and relate to open source in very different ways. You seem adamant on framing open source as a dichotomy of collaboration and competition. Winners and losers. One banner or the other. I believe this is a false dichotomy caused by the very same tribalism mindset I am criticizing.

> Imagine a world where those projects had no name, no formal organization, no codes of conduct, no common banner. Is that a better world?

All of these things are present when you go to a theme park, or buy something in a shop, or visit my house. Interacting with these places does not make you part of a "tribe" or put you under a "banner".

I can go to this shop today, and tomorrow to another one. There is no need for me to entangle my own identity with either of them to enjoy them for what they are.

This is what I consider my projects to be. Little places for people to meet and work together when they feel like it. They are not tribes.

> Collaboration is inherently political (and therefore tribal). We will come up with words (and yes banners) to (lossily) describe our values, and choose which banners to work under that describe our values.

Collaboration isn't inherently tribal. It can happen at a small scale, on specific topics, and during a short amount of time. There is also no full alignment of values needed to cooperate. That's the beauty of it.

> To reframe this, what if this wasn't about what the "producer" is entitled to, but rather how you think you should treat them? Should someone giving away free gifts be treated with respect and collaborated with, or competed with? Would you try to consider their human feelings (and not operate under the assumption that they are fully enlightened?). Would an enlightened person comport themselves as if everyone else is enlightened?

As I said, this feels like a false dichotomy. There is no competition.

Me giving away more "free gifts" cannot ever be considered "competing" with someone else that is also giving away "free gifts".

The only way for someone to conclude that is if the original gifts are not truly "free", but come with some "hidden" expectations attached to them.

> Feel free to leave one more response to what I've said, but I'll refrain from responding further on these more abstract issues, and I will ask that everyone else does the same, in the interest of this thread not devolving.

No worries. Happy to leave it here! I enjoyed the conversation. Thank you for taking the time!

comments.author: participant3
comments.body:
@participant2 

I was going to soften my response, but after reading through your responses, I think my initial reaction was justified.

Bevy and Dioxus have been collaborating on a library called [Taffy](http://github.com/dioxusLabs/taffy) for two years now. It was the sheer fact that I revived the original stretch project that @participant1 took note and helped Dioxus get corporate sponsorship, enabling me to go full time. Now, Taffy has 2,700,981 downloads, more than Bevy, Dioxus, Iced, etc and powers many projects like the popular [Zed](https://zed.dev) editor. I am forever grateful - my life has taken a different direction since that initial email.

The fact that Bevy understands the nuance of open source means their project has been more successful than the rest. And it really informs my view on open source. My father likens people who see the world as zero sum games as "crabs in a pot." If we continue to step on each other in the ecosystem, we will never see "escape velocity." As popular as Bevy is, libraries like Next.js see 10m downloads a WEEK, and React sees 5 million a DAY. Iced has 845k in its entire lifetime. We exist in a nascent space.

Our goal with the subsecond engine is to spin it out into a library for a "white label experience." But it is not done yet. We have Dioxus 0.7 we want to get out very soon. It doesn't make sense for us to build cargo subcommand that we will never use. If you want to use subsecond today in its full glory, then `dx serve --hotpatch` is the way right now. In the future, `bevy run --hotpatch` might be a thing too. I would love to see `dx` evolve to be similar to Vue's Vite. I hate watching the Rust ecosystem continue to reinvent the wheel and it would be good for us to work together on shared build tooling. 

Entitlement runs very strong in open source, and everyone in this thread with no skin in the game does not understand what it means to run a company in open source land. I have no shovels to sell you, sadly, but if you think you are entitled for Dioxus to build tools it will never use, then you really don't understand how running a company works.

I suggested a "cargo plus" because I don't believe cargo will ever add something like subsecond to the default user experience. It is too opinionated, too complex, too unstable, there are dragons, people don't like our UI, etc. It's a shame that you cannot run  `cargo run` a WASM app, but I've been to RustNL for three years now, and I can tell you the cargo team does not have bandwidth or funding to stabilize any of this work. I've been told "we love what you do, but we love that you do it over there."

By taking our work wholesale and then distributing it to your users, you gave them hotpatching... but you also burned good will with the people who raised capital, started a company, became experts in binary patching, and then distributed a massively transformative technology for free. You can `dx serve` an iced app. It will be an extremely polished user experience. We will market `dx` as a generic cargo runner soon enough and users will prefer it. 

I want hot-patching to be seen as a communal technology by the ecosystem and find a management structure to it similar to for Taffy. My goal with it was to distribute it as widely as possible in the Rust ecosystem. A rising tide lifts all boats. Having the support - both social and technical - of another large Rust GUI project would be fantastic. But, when the authors of those projects don't truly understand the ethos of open source and burn their goodwill, it makes me never want to work with them in the future.

comments.author: participant10
comments.body:
@participant3 

> Instead of reaching out with an offer to help modularize the subsecond engine, you went straight to copy-pasting our code into a new project, stripping it down, renaming it, and then started shopping around for help to maintain it. Why not work with us directly? I hope you see how this insulting to our team, especially coming from a project lead.

You're complaining about someone experimenting on open source software in their own private repo for a handful of hours as if they had slapped their branding on your product as-is and started distributing it to general users. Which, by the way, your license would allow for, but is not the case here. Note it's `participant2/cargo-hot` not `iced-rs/cargo-hot`.

I also see no evidence of anyone "shopping around for maintainers". Ironically and tragically, if anything this discussion has a chilling effect on people trying considering contributing to this ecosystem.

Whether you choose to feel insulted is besides the point. You have sufficient agency to choose to engage collaboratively instead.

I get that you built something *really cool* and you want full credit for it. Nobody is trying to take that away! But you're complaining about a developer not working with you directly and yet all you've done is encourage people to not work with you directly.

Generally I only find criticism productive if it comes with a suggestion for improvement. What exactly are you suggesting?

Maybe let's focus less on how insulted we feel and more on what we imagine the ideal future to look like in a way that maximizes the benefits to the Rust ecosystem, and then work towards that. I think we'll find much more common ground if we spend our energy there instead.
